headline: US refiners run flat out as diesel stays tight, and Singapore's fuel oil tanks fill
paragraphs: US refineries ran at 97.5% of capacity in the week to 20 Nov, up from 95.7% the week before and 92.3% a year ago. Running that hard soaks up crude, yet commercial crude stocks still rose 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million, about 2% below a year ago. Cushing, the delivery point for WTI futures, slipped 0.5 million barrels to 25.6 million, while the Strategic Petroleum Reserve fell another 2.9 million barrels to 273.5 million, a third lower than a year ago.

The products side is where it gets interesting. Gasoline rose 1.7 million barrels and is now 3.7% above last year, which is comfortable going into winter. Distillates, which covers diesel and heating oil, added only 0.7 million barrels and sit 5.9% below a year ago despite refiners running near full tilt. That gap helps explain why the US crack spread is still wide: refiners are being paid to keep making diesel.

In Singapore, Enterprise Singapore data for the week to 18 Nov showed total onshore oil product stocks down 1.1% to 39.93 million barrels. Light distillates such as naphtha and gasoline fell to a near two-month low of 10.8 million barrels and middle distillates eased to 8.33 million, while residual fuel oil jumped 6.5% to 20.81 million barrels. Shipping fuel supplier ENGINE says residual stocks have averaged about 9% higher in November than in October, helped by higher net fuel oil imports.

The common thread is middle distillates. Both the US and Singapore are holding less diesel than a year ago, so any refinery outage or cold snap would show up there first. Fuel oil, by contrast, is building up in Asia's main bunkering hub, which should take some pressure off marine fuel prices for now.
period: US: week to 20 Nov 2026 (EIA, released 25 Nov). Singapore: week to 18 Nov 2026 (Enterprise Singapore). mb = million barrels
